newsitem.title: GERMANY: SPD leaders agree demands before German tax talks.
newsitem.headline: SPD leaders agree demands before German tax talks.

text.p: Leaders of Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD), focusing on lowering social security contributions, on Monday adopted a catalogue of demands they would put to the Bonn coalition at crunch tax talks on Tuesday.
"All decisions that are reached to reduce unemployment, we will go along with," said SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine.

Above all the party wanted the social security contributions deducted from German paycheques to fall by two percentage points starting July 1. Germans give up about 42 percent of their wages to job insurance, pension and health plan contributions.
The reduction would lead to the creation of 200,000 jobs, the SPD said in a position paper, adding that it would accept little room for compromise on this point.
German unemployment eased by 190,000 in March, but remained at a near-record level of 4.3 million.

Bonn also wanted to lower labour costs to create jobs, and proposed to balance reductions with a one percentage point increase in the value-added tax to 16 percent, or a rise in fuel tax to finance the cuts.

In its paper, the SPD also said it wanted no income taxes on income up to 14,000 marks for single wage-earners and 28,000 marks for married couples, a 30 mark increase in child subsidies and an entry-level tax rate of less than 20 percent.
Reductions in other subsidies would offset those measures, Lafontaine said, adding that only a "fully financed tax reform was possible."
The coalition has proposed tax-free income up to 13,000 marks for individuals and 26,000 marks for couples, and wants to leave the subsidies at 220 marks per child for a family's first two children.
It has proposed lowering to entry income tax rate to 15 percent from 26 percent, and the top rate to 39 percent from 53 percent.
